title: Majestic Pawn Chase
reviewNotes: Verified the final six-piece blockade from Black’s side. The tempo-preserving pawn move wins; tablebase also shows Kf2 wins, correcting the source’s claim that g6 is unique.
transcript: After pawn to h3, black is only two steps away from getting a new queen, and it doesn't seem like white has any way to stop that. But as it turns out, this is not as simple as it might seem. This white knight has two ways to try and approach the black pawn. The first one, knight to d6, fails. After pawn to h2, white can give a check to the black king and then get one step closer. But actually, after king to f3, black is attacking the knight. The white king cannot defend it in any way, and after the knight jumps to the corner, the black king is going to attack it and take away all squares. So, black would win. But white does have a different way to get closer via d4. And if black is not careful and simply pushes the pawn now, there is going to be a knight fork attacking the king and pawn and drawing the game. But black is not that naive and instead plays king to e3, making it much harder for the white knight to approach the pawn. And for a second here, it seems like black is simply out of the woods. Does white have no way to stop the pawn? Well, not exactly. White can play the very surprising king to g4, attacking the black pawn and leaving the white knight to hang. Because, of course, if the knight is taken, this would be a drawn king and pawn endgame. So, instead, black has to push the h2 pawn and try to now get closer to the promotion. But of course, moving the white king has freed up the f5 square for the knight, which comes in with another check. And now, after the king moves, the knight can jump to g3 with the help of the king and prevent the promotion. But black is not a fool, and he does play on with king to g2, preventing the knight from jumping to the corner and realizing that if the white king ever moves, he's going to be able to pick up the white knight and win the game. But of course, the white king can just stay defending the knight, and there is never going to be a way to kick him out. Because after a g5 check, for example, the king can simply come back, stay defending the knight, and black is actually in zugzwang. He has to either move this pawn or the king, but if the pawn moves, the white knight is going to take it. And if the king moves, the white king is going to walk in and always keep the black king out of the corner, and this is going to be a draw. But you see, very often endgames are decided by just one tempo. And what seems counterintuitive turns out to be the solution to this position. If we could land the g-pawn on g5 when the king [music] is on g4, then the situation would be completely different. And so that means that the only winning move in this position is the patient and precise pawn to g6, only taking one step, but allowing the white king to come back to g4, and then playing g5, because this time it is white that is in zugzwang. The white king cannot stay on either of these squares defending the knight, and the knight cannot move because it has to defend the promotion square. So after either one of them moves, black is simply going to win this beautiful endgame.
